1 Iam Origenis placitum fuerat ὅτι οἱ ἀστέρες οὐκ εἰσὶ ποιητικοὶ τῶν ἐν ἀνθρώ-
ποις, σημαντικοὶ δὲ μόνον. Cf. Bouché-Leclercq, Astrol. grecque, p. 614, n. 2.
Hanc sententiam defendit saeculo VI Procopius Gazaeus (Mai, Classici auctores,
VI, p. 73 s.); at Stephanum Byzantinum fontem Manuelis esse crediderim, vide
Catal., II, p. 185. Cf. infra p. 122, 34. De eadem doctrina apud veteres astrologos
et philosophos, cf. Boll, Stud. über Ptolem., 1894, p. 221, 1.
sections.en: 1 Already it had been the opinion of Origen that the stars are not productive of the things in men, but only significant. Cf. Bouché-Leclercq, Astrol. grecque, p. 614, n. 2. This opinion was defended in the 6th century by Procopius of Gaza (Mai, Classici auctores, VI, p. 73 f.); but I would believe that Stephanus of Byzantium is the source of Manuel, see Catal., II, p. 185. Cf. below p. 122, 34. On the same doctrine among ancient astrologers and philosophers, cf. Boll, Stud. über Ptolem., 1894, p. 221, 1.

summary.headline: Stars as Signs, Not Causes
summary.text: Manuel’s Christian critique of astrology distinguishes stars as signs rather than causes: natural observation of their powers, mixtures, and configurations is useful, while invoking stars, relying on predictions instead of prayer and good works, and excessive curiosity are impious. A note traces this doctrine from Origen through Procopius of Gaza and Stephanus of Byzantium.
